pageCache.pageTitle: Welcome to Windlesham House School in West Sussex
pageCache.text:
Welcome to Windlesham House School
Curiosity is at the heart of every child
At Windlesham House, we believe every child has the potential to thrive. Our role is to nurture curious minds, inspire confidence and encourage children to embrace opportunities with enthusiasm and courage.
A breath of fresh air
Our bespoke admissions process focuses on the needs of each child and their family. As a ‘gently selective’ school, Windlesham House’s excellent record continues to prepare children for outstanding day and boarding senior schools.
Living at Windlesham House
We understand there’s no place like home but we are proud to offer a nurturing environment where children are happy, well cared for and truly flourish while living, learning and playing at Windlesham House.
Why families choose Windlesham
Children are genuinely known Because every child deserves to feel seen, understood and encouraged to become the very best version of themselves.
Exceptional opportunities every day From sport and performing arts to outdoor learning and over 150 co-curricular activities, children are encouraged to discover new passions and hidden talents.
Outstanding pastoral care A warm, supportive environment where happiness, wellbeing and confidence are at the heart of every school day.
A childhood to remember Set within 70 acres of beautiful Sussex countryside, children have the freedom to explore, play and grow.
Preparing for life beyond Windlesham Academic excellence, character, curiosity and confidence combine to ensure every child is ready for the next stage of their journey.
Where every child discovers a love of sport
At Windlesham House, our view is that sports are all about games – and games should be fun! Our approach is that if a child works their socks off but the outcome is not quite what they had hoped for, we look at the value in the process rather than focusing on the target that was not reached.
Take a look at our facilities

Our communication with parents is a partnership we treasure and one that enhances every child’s success.”

At Windlesham, every child is helped to achieve their very best through an excellent all-round education, giving them the strongest possible start in life.”

pageCache.pageTitle: Choosing the right independent school in West Sussex: a parent’s guide - Windlesham House School
pageCache.text:
Choosing a school is one of the biggest decisions a family makes. With so many options across the county, finding the right independent school in West Sussex can feel daunting. The good news is that when you know what to look for, and you trust your instincts on a visit, the right school often has a way of making itself known. Here is a simple guide to help.
What should I look for in an independent school?
Start with the things that shape a child’s everyday happiness: the quality of pastoral care, the size of classes, and whether staff seem to genuinely know the children. Academic results matter, of course, but so does the atmosphere. Are children engaged and confident? Do they seem to enjoy being there? A good independent school should stretch children academically while giving them the space and support to be themselves.
Day, boarding or both?
Think about the shape of your family life. Some children thrive as day pupils, home each evening; others love the friendships and independence that boarding brings. Many schools, including ours, offer full, weekly and flexi boarding, so you are not locked into one path. It is worth choosing a school that gives you the flexibility to change your mind as your child grows.
How important is the setting?
More than many parents expect. A school’s surroundings shape the kind of childhood on offer. Space to run, climb and explore, room for sport and the outdoors, and a general sense of calm all make a real difference to how children learn and feel. Set in 70 acres of the South Downs near Pulborough, we see every day how much a green, generous setting adds to a child’s education.
What questions should I ask on a visit?
A visit is your best chance to see behind the prospectus. Ask how the school helps children settle, how it supports those who find something difficult, and how it stretches those who race ahead. Ask what happens beyond the classroom, and where pupils go on to next. And notice the small things: how staff interact with children, whether the pupils showing you round seem proud of their school and whether it feels like somewhere your child would be happy.
How do I know a school is right for my child?
In the end, the right school is the one where you can picture your child thriving. Reports and results tell part of the story, but nothing replaces the feeling you get walking around and meeting the community. Trust that instinct. At Windlesham House, our leavers move on to a wide range of leading senior schools at 13+ and Common Entrance, but what families remember most is how happy and well known their children felt while they were with us.
Come and see us. If you are exploring independent schools in West Sussex, we would love to show you ours. Book a place at an autumn open morning or arrange a private tour to see how Windlesham House feels like home.
At Windlesham House, we don’t simply prepare children for the future, we give them a childhood worth remembering. Discover a school where curiosity is nurtured, every child is genuinely known and childhood is celebrated every day.

pageCache.pageTitle: Learning enrichment | Private School | Windlesham House School
pageCache.text:
Supporting every pupil to reach their full potential
Our learning enrichment department ensures that every pupil, regardless of their learning profile, can access the curriculum and thrive at Windlesham House. We celebrate differences and provide tailored support that builds confidence and independence.
How does Windlesham House support pupils with additional learning needs?
We recognize that children learn in different ways and at different paces. Some pupils benefit from additional support to help them access the curriculum fully, while others need extension and enrichment. Our learning enrichment department, led by Melissa Jordan, provides expert support tailored to individual needs.
Support might be needed for a range of reasons including dyslexia, dyscalculia, dysgraphia, dyspraxia, attention difficulties, processing speed differences, or working memory challenges. We also support pupils who are exceptionally able and need differentiated provision to remain challenged and engaged.
Boosting self-esteem and self-confidence
We work not only to boost children’s self-esteem and self-confidence but to also capitalise on and increase on their strengths. We have close contact with other educational and health-related professionals if more information, guidance and support is needed.
Our well-resourced department is actively involved in our school community. The team works closely with the subject teachers and pastoral staff to ensure that the learning experiences are maximised throughout all aspects of school life.
We love to see the children develop into confident people who understand their areas of difficulty and know how to develop strategies to compensate for and overcome certain weaknesses.
What types of support are available?
Assessment and identification
When pupils join Windlesham House, we conduct baseline assessments to understand their learning strengths and areas for development. If teachers or parents have concerns about a pupil’s progress, we can conduct further diagnostic assessments. We work with external educational psychologists when specialist assessment is needed.
Individual support sessions
Pupils who would benefit from additional help receive regular one-to-one or small group sessions with our learning enrichment specialists. These sessions focus on specific areas such as:
Organizational skills and executive function support
Touch-typing and assistive technology training
Exam access arrangements preparation
In-class support
Our learning enrichment assistants work alongside subject teachers in lessons, providing discreet support to pupils who need it. This ensures pupils remain fully integrated in their classes while receiving appropriate help to access learning.
Differentiation and reasonable adjustments
All teachers receive training in differentiating lessons and making reasonable adjustments for pupils with additional needs. This might include modified worksheets, additional processing time, use of assistive technology or alternative ways of demonstrating understanding.
Individual Learning Plans
Pupils receiving learning enrichment support have individual learning plans that outline their strengths, areas for development, and strategies that help them learn effectively. These plans are shared with all staff and reviewed regularly with parents.
How do you support pupils who are exceptionally able?
Exceptionally able pupils also benefit from learning enrichment provision. We ensure these pupils are sufficiently challenged through curriculum extension, enrichment activities, and opportunities to explore subjects in greater depth. This might include
Acceleration in specific subjects where appropriate
Participation in academic competitions and Olympiads
Independent research projects on topics of interest
Mentoring relationships with subject specialists
Preparation for senior school scholarship examinations
What is the philosophy behind learning enrichment?
We believe that additional learning needs should never be barriers to success. With the right support and strategies, all pupils can achieve their potential and develop confidence in themselves as learners. Our approach focuses on
Building on strengths
We identify what pupils do well and use these strengths as foundations for development. Celebrating success builds confidence and motivation
Developing independence
Our goal is to give pupils strategies they can use independently. We gradually reduce support as pupils become more confident and self-sufficient
Whole-school approach
Learning enrichment is not just the responsibility of specialists. All staff understand and implement strategies that support diverse learners
Partnership with parents
We work closely with families, sharing strategies and ensuring consistency between school and home support
How are exam access arrangements managed?
For pupils who require exam access arrangements (such as additional time, use of a reader or scribe, rest breaks, or use of a word processor), we conduct appropriate assessments and apply to senior schools and exam boards on behalf of families. We ensure pupils are familiar with using any arrangements before sitting actual examinations.
Is there an additional charge for learning enrichment support?
Yes, individual and small group learning enrichment sessions incur an additional charge. The cost depends on the frequency and duration of sessions required. In-class support and whole-school differentiation are included in school fees. We discuss support needs and associated costs with parents before provision begins.
Will my child be withdrawn from lessons for learning enrichment?
We aim to minimize disruption to learning. Where possible, sessions are scheduled during non-core lesson times such as during games afternoons, co-curricular slots, or registration periods. If withdrawal from lessons is necessary, we rotate sessions to ensure minimal impact on any single subject and communicate clearly with parents about the rationale.
How do you communicate with parents about progress?
Parents of pupils receiving learning enrichment support receive regular updates via email or telephone. Individual Learning Plans are reviewed at least termly with parents invited to contribute. Progress is also reported in main school reports. We welcome ongoing dialogue and respond promptly to parent queries.
Discussing support needs
If you think your child might benefit from learning enrichment support, please contact our head of learning enrichment, Melissa Jordan, at whsoffice@windlesham.com or speak with the admissions team who can arrange a consultation.

pageCache.pageTitle: Pre-prep curriculum | Pulborough | Windlesham House School
pageCache.text:
Outstanding provision from Reception to Year 2
Children are immersed in rich, dynamic learning experiences every day. From exploring swimming and art with specialist teachers to embarking on magical storytelling journeys, each day is a fresh opportunity to spark imagination, build confidence, and express themselves.
What makes Windlesham House curriculum stand out?
Children dive into a whirlwind of hands-on learning, from exploring the depths of swimming, art, cooking, computing and music with specialist teachers to venturing into the great outdoors at forest school. They embark on magical storytelling journeys with visiting authors and dazzle in whole-school creative performances. Each day is a fresh opportunity to spark their imagination, build confidence and express themselves in new and exciting ways.
We believe children flourish when they are encouraged to ask questions, explore new ideas, and express themselves in a safe, supportive environment. These values guide our approach to teaching, relationships, and expectations, fostering a community where every child feels seen, valued, and motivated to succeed.
What modern learning approaches does the school use?
An evolving education
We have made purposeful changes to our physical environment and curriculum to better meet the evolving needs of our children. After careful research and observation, we redesigned our classrooms to create calm, open spaces that support movement, focus, and independence. Walls were repainted a soothing sage green to reduce sensory overload, and traditional furniture was replaced with flexi-seating. This has empowered pupils, particularly boys, to take ownership of how they learn best, reducing frustration and increasing engagement.
Flexi-seating initiative
Our innovative flexi-seating approach allows children to choose learning positions that work best for them, whether sitting at traditional desks, standing at high tables, or working on floor cushions. This freedom helps children develop self-awareness about their learning preferences while maintaining focus and engagement.
Languages and cultural learning
This year, we have introduced a new language model to better prepare children for their journey through prep school. A 2-year rolling programme covers 6 languages, with each taught by a single pre-prep teacher to the Reception to Year Two cohort. This ensures consistency, progression, and a clear link with the prep school curriculum. Lessons focus on culture as well as vocabulary, using familiar resources like games and flashcards to create a joyful, holistic approach to language learning.
Languages explored include French, Spanish, German, Mandarin, Italian and Latin. Each language is taught within cultural context, helping children understand different traditions, celebrations, and ways of life around the world.
How is the curriculum structured across year groups?
Reception (age 4 – 5)
Our Reception year follows the Early Years Foundation Stage framework, focusing on learning through play and exploration. Children develop foundational skills in literacy and numeracy while building social and emotional capabilities. The curriculum emphasizes personal, social, and emotional development alongside communication and language skills.
Children engage in themed learning that captures their imagination, from exploring minibeasts in the school grounds to learning about people who help us in our community. Phonics teaching begins systematically, and children are introduced to early mathematical concepts through practical, hands-on activities.
Year 1 (age 5 – 6)
Year 1 marks the transition from play-based learning to more structured lessons while maintaining joy and creativity. Children build on their phonics knowledge and begin reading independently. Mathematics becomes more formal, introducing addition, subtraction, and number patterns. Topic-based learning links subjects together, such as exploring castles through history, art, writing, and construction activities.
Specialist lessons increase in Year 1, with children receiving dedicated teaching in Physical Education, music, computing, and swimming. Forest school sessions continue to provide outdoor learning opportunities that develop resilience and environmental awareness.
Year 2 (age 6 to 7)
Year 2 consolidates and extends learning across all curriculum areas. Children develop greater independence in their work and are encouraged to apply skills across different contexts. Literacy skills expand to include different writing genres, while mathematics introduces more complex problem-solving. Science investigations become more hands-on with children learning about materials, plants, animals and simple forces.
This year represents an important bridge to prep school, with children developing study skills, organizational abilities and greater academic confidence. We introduce more formal assessment to understand each child’s strengths and areas for development as they prepare for Year 3.
What subjects do children study in pre-prep?
Core subjects
English (reading, writing, phonics, speaking and listening)
Mathematics (number, calculation, measurement, geometry)
Science (biology, materials, seasonal changes)
Foundation subjects
History and geography
Art and design
Design and technology
Computing
Specialist subjects
Physical education and games
Swimming
Music (including instrument introduction)
Drama and performance
Enrichment
Forest school
Languages (six-language rotation)
Personal, social, health education
How do you assess progress in pre-prep?
We use ongoing formative assessment through observation, conversation and reviewing children’s work. Parents receive regular updates through our communication app, termly written reports rather than comparing children against each other.
Do you follow the National Curriculum?
We follow the Early Years Foundation Stage framework for Reception and use the National Curriculum as a foundation for Years 1 & 2. However, as an independent school, we have the freedom to enrich and extend beyond these frameworks, ensuring our curriculum meets the needs of our children and prepares them excellently for prep school.
How do children transition from pre-prep to prep?
We ensure a seamless transition from Year 2 to Year 3 through careful preparation in the summer term. Children visit prep classrooms, meet their new teachers and learn about new routines. Our pre-prep and prep teams work closely together to share information about each child’s learning style, strengths and areas for development.
Curriculum overview
Our curriculum overview documents for each year group are available from the admissions office, providing detailed information about what your child will learn throughout the year.

pageCache.pageTitle: Read Write Inc. Phonics | Windlesham House School
pageCache.text:
Confident readers become confident learners.
Here at Windlesham, we are proud to teach phonics and early reading using the Read Write Inc. (RWI) programme. This carefully structured approach helps children build reading confidence, independence and fluency from the very start, equipping them with the skills they need to become lifelong readers who love reading for pleasure.
Why do we teach phonics with Read Write Inc.?
Read Write Inc. is a nationally recognised phonics programme designed to help children learn to read quickly and successfully. Through systematic phonics teaching, engaging texts and consistent daily practice, our pupils develop a strong foundation that enables them to thrive as readers, writers and learners.
What do our children say?
“I love phonics, it is amazing and so much fun! My favourite thing about phonics is when we practice our nonsense words, we always say ‘What a load of nonsense!’.”
“Phonics has helped me with my spelling – I didn’t realise there was so many different ways we could spell the same sound for example ‘j’, ‘g’, ‘ge’ and ‘dge’ all make the same sound!”
“It has helped us with tricky words and sounding out new words in our head.”
How do we teach phonics at Windlesham?
Phonics sits at the heart of our pre-prep curriculum, and our daily teaching reflects that commitment. Our experienced phonics teachers deliver engaging, high-quality lessons every day, making sure that learning is both purposeful and enjoyable.
All pupils are carefully grouped according to their phonics knowledge and understanding, so that teaching is precisely matched to each child’s next steps. This targeted approach means every pupil feels supported, challenged and successful. Alongside their daily sessions, children read one-to-one with their class teachers twice each week. These frequent opportunities to practise and apply their skills build fluency, deepen comprehension and strengthen reading confidence.
How does phonics connect to reading and writing?
Phonics learning reaches far beyond discrete lessons and is fully embedded within our wider English curriculum. During weekly writing sessions, children apply the sounds and skills they have learned, writing with increasing independence and accuracy. It is always a joy to watch pupils grow into confident writers, unlocking their creativity and imagination as they realise they can express their own ideas on the page.
What happens as children move into prep?
Our aim is that every child leaves pre-prep as a confident, capable reader, fully prepared for the transition into prep school. To ensure continuity and consistency, all lower prep classrooms are equipped with Read Write Inc. resources, allowing pupils to keep applying their phonics knowledge as they move into the next stage of their learning journey. This seamless transition supports children’s confidence, independence and success as they begin life in the prep school.
What impact are we already seeing?
Throughout this year, the impact has been remarkable. Across the pre-prep, pupils are showing growing confidence, enthusiasm and independence in their reading and writing. Children are eager to read, proud to share their achievements and increasingly fluent when applying their phonics knowledge, both in lessons and beyond the classroom.
Teachers have observed significant gains in reading confidence and engagement, with pupils approaching new texts with excitement and resilience. The consistency of our approach across year groups has created a strong culture of reading, where success is celebrated and every child feels empowered as a learner. We are incredibly proud of the progress our pupils are making, and we look forward to building on this strong foundation as our phonics journey continues to grow.
What do our parents say?
“We have been so pleased with the impact Read Write Inc. has had on both of our children. It has been a truly positive experience for them. The clear and consistent approach has really supported their learning and built their confidence. We have noticed a big difference in their phonics skills and, most importantly, it’s been wonderful to see them pick up a book because they want to read, and read it independently.”
“I am genuinely impressed with how well both of my children are reading. I just wanted to say how blown away we are by our child’s progress since introducing Read Write Inc. The improvement in both his reading and confidence has honestly been incredible to see. Our son now seems to find sounding out words so easy and natural, and we’ve noticed he is mostly sight reading now, which feels like such a huge step forward. More than anything, his confidence with reading has grown so much, and he seems genuinely proud of himself, which has been lovely to watch. We really feel the new phonics approach has had such a positive impact on him, and we’re incredibly grateful to all the teachers for the support and encouragement they’ve given him.”
At Windlesham House, we don’t simply prepare children for the future, we give them a childhood worth remembering. Discover a school where curiosity is nurtured, every child is genuinely known and childhood is celebrated every day.
Book your place at our next open morning.

pageCache.pageTitle: Prep curriculum | Prep School | Windlesham House School
pageCache.text:
Comprehensive academic programme for Years 3 – 8
Our curriculum is creative, engaging, and accessible. We balance academic rigour with innovation, ensuring pupils achieve their potential while developing genuine love for learning that extends far beyond examinations.
What makes Windlesham House curriculum stand out?
Academic rigour and challenge are important at Windlesham House. We want all pupils to achieve their potential within a supportive environment where learning is creative, engaging, and accessible. Our curriculum goes beyond preparing pupils for examinations, developing skills, knowledge, and attitudes that serve them throughout life.
All academic subjects are taught in well-equipped specialist areas by teachers with passion for their subjects. This specialist approach ensures depth of knowledge and teaching expertise while allowing cross-curricular links that enrich understanding.
What subjects do pupils study?
Core subjects
English
Pupils develop advanced literacy skills through exposure to rich, challenging texts. Creative writing flourishes alongside analytical skills. Drama techniques enhance speaking and listening. By Year 8, pupils confidently handle complex literature and produce sophisticated written work across multiple genres.
Mathematics
Our mathematics curriculum builds deep understanding rather than superficial procedural knowledge. Pupils learn to think mathematically, applying problem-solving skills to unfamiliar situations. Setting by ability ensures appropriate challenge. Regular practice develops fluency while investigations promote deeper thinking.
Science
Taught in four purpose-built laboratories by specialist teachers, science at Windlesham House is hands on and inquiry based. Pupils conduct experiments, analyse data, and draw evidence-based conclusions. Biology, chemistry and physics are taught as separate disciplines from Year 7 preparing pupils excellently for senior school science.
Languages, culture, and linguistics
We have reimagined our modern foreign languages department as Languages, Culture, and Linguistics (LCL). This innovative programme prepares pupils to become confident, curious global citizens.
Years 3- 6
Pupils study both French and Spanish, switching halfway through the academic year. Lessons are vibrant and interactive, focusing on speaking, listening and cultural understanding. Our approach emphasizes high-frequency vocabulary that allows pupils to communicate effectively from early on.
Years 7 & 8
The LCL diploma programme blends language provision with exciting strands in linguistics and global culture. Pupils explore how language actually works, developing curiosity about patterns and structures. Research projects on global culture broaden horizons and build research skills.
Humanities
History
Chronological study from ancient civilizations to modern history develops historical understanding and analytical skills. Pupils learn to evaluate sources, construct arguments, and understand cause and consequence. Local history and school archives provide tangible connections to the past.
Geography
Physical and human geography are explored through case studies, fieldwork, and contemporary issues. Map skills develop alongside understanding of global challenges such as climate change, population growth, and resource management.
Religious Studies
Pupils explore major world religions, ethical issues and philosophical questions. The focus is on understanding diverse beliefs and developing reasoned opinions while respecting different viewpoints.
Philosophy and ethics
Introduced in Years 7 & 8, this subject develops critical thinking through exploring fundamental questions about knowledge, existence, morality and truth.
Creative arts
Art
Spacious, well-lit studios provide inspiring environments for exploring drawing, painting, printmaking, sculpture, and mixed media. Pupils study artists from different periods and cultures while developing their own creative voice.
Design and Technology
Modern workshops equipped with laser cutters, 3D printers and traditional tools enable pupils to design and make products. Projects span resistant materials, textiles and food technology, developing practical skills and design thinking.
Music
All pupils receive classroom music education covering theory, composition, and appreciation. Individual instrumental and vocal lessons are available across numerous instruments. Ensembles, choirs, and orchestras provide performance opportunities for all abilities.
Drama
Drama lessons develop confidence, creativity, and collaboration. Pupils explore different theatrical styles, techniques, and texts. Regular productions showcase talent while building teamwork and performance skills.
Physical education
PE is a core subject throughout the prep years. Pupils develop fitness, skills and tactical understanding across numerous sports. Competitive opportunities exist for all abilities through house competitions and inter-school fixtures. The focus is on enjoyment, improvement and lifelong participation rather than solely on elite performance.
Digital learning
Computing is taught as a specialist subject covering computer science, information technology, and digital citizenship. Pupils learn coding, develop applications, and gain essential digital literacy skills. From Year 6 onwards, our bring your own device programme enables seamless integration of technology across the curriculum.
Personal, social, health education (PSHE)
PSHE provides dedicated time for pupils to develop personal awareness, healthy relationships, understanding of diversity and life skills. Age-appropriate topics include wellbeing, safety, relationships, financial literacy and preparation for senior school.
How is the curriculum delivered?
Years 3 – 6
Pupils experience a broad, balanced curriculum with increasing specialist teaching as they progress. Form tutors maintain pastoral oversight while subject specialists deliver lessons. Homework gradually increases, developing independent study skills.
Years 7 & 8
All teaching is by subject specialists. The distinctive Diploma Programme provides additional breadth and depth. Pupils prepare for senior school entrance examinations and scholarship opportunities.
How do you extend the most able pupils?
Our scholars programme supports high-achieving pupils with bespoke learning pathways. This might include acceleration, enrichment activities, mentoring, and targeted preparation for senior school scholarships. Pupils work beyond their year group curriculum where appropriate, ensuring continual challenge and engagement.
How much homework do pupils receive?
Homework increases gradually through the years. Year 3 pupils might spend 30 minutes per evening, increasing to 90 minutes by Year 8. Boarders complete homework (prep) at school under staff supervision. Day pupils may stay for prep sessions if convenient for families.
Do you prepare pupils for 11+ and 13+ examinations?
Yes, we have outstanding success preparing pupils for senior school entrance examinations at both 11+ and 13+. The curriculum naturally aligns with these requirements, and additional targeted sessions ensure pupils are examination-ready. Our 100% first-choice placement record demonstrates the effectiveness of our preparation.
How do you assess pupil progress?
We use continuous formative assessment alongside more formal testing. Regular feedback helps pupils understand their progress and next steps. Parents receive detailed written reports each term plus parent consultation meetings. Internal examinations in Years 6 – 8 prepare pupils for senior school entrance assessments.
Curriculum overview
Detailed curriculum overview documents for each year group are available from the school office. These provide termly breakdowns of topics studied in each subject.

pageCache.pageTitle: Geography lessons on our doorstep - Windlesham House School
pageCache.text:
Year 8 enjoyed a fascinating geography field trip to visit our neighbours at Wiston Estate. The children were engaged, thoughtful and curious throughout the day as they explored a range of geographical and environmental topics.
During the first part of the visit, Richard guided the group around the estate, discussing issues ranging from global farming challenges and the impact of the Rampion Offshore Wind Farm to the remarkable journey of swallows as they prepare for their annual migration to warmer climates. The pupils asked insightful questions and demonstrated a keen interest in the connections between the local landscape and wider global issues.
In the second session, Kirsty explained why the chalk downland surrounding Wiston provides the ideal conditions for growing vines. The children learned that this year’s warm and sunny weather had created excellent growing conditions for the grapes, leading to an earlier-than-usual harvest.
The group was then given a tour of the winery, where they saw the impressive French grape press and learned about the fermentation process that transforms grape juice into sparkling wine. While they were not able to sample the finished product, they did enjoy the opportunity to seek out and taste grapes straight from the vines.
The children were impeccably behaved throughout the visit and showed great enthusiasm for their learning, making detailed notes to support their geography diploma projects. Richard and Kirsty both commented on how much they enjoy hosting Windlesham pupils and were particularly impressed by the curiosity and thoughtful questions of Bosco, Philo and Tommy, who deserve special recognition.
It was a valuable and memorable experience, giving the children the opportunity to see geography in action and deepen their understanding of the relationship between people, industry and the environment.
At Windlesham House, we don’t simply prepare children for the future, we give them a childhood worth remembering. Discover a school where curiosity is nurtured, every child is genuinely known and childhood is celebrated every day.

pageCache.pageTitle: EAL (English as an Additional Language) | Windlesham House School
pageCache.text:
Supporting international pupils to thrive
Windlesham House welcomes pupils from around the world. Our specialist EAL programme ensures international pupils develop English language skills quickly and confidently while fully participating in school life.
How does Windlesham House support EAL learners?
Through our EAL programme, we aim to improve English skills across all four key areas: reading, writing, speaking and listening. We also develop understanding of English grammar, pronunciation, vocabulary and discourse structures. Our goal is for each child to function happily and successfully in both classroom and social situations.
It is very important to us that children from non-English speaking backgrounds start to communicate as soon as possible. This happens quickly as children make friends and join in Windlesham House life. We work on improving grammatical accuracy as children gain confidence with fluency.
What EAL teaching is provided?
Individual and small group lessons
Our EAL teaching is delivered by specialist teachers through bespoke one-to-one lessons and small group sessions. These focused sessions allow us to target specific language needs and provide intensive support matched to each pupil’s level.
Lesson content is tailored to individual needs and might include
Phonics and pronunciation practice
Vocabulary building including academic and subject-specific terms
Grammar instruction and practice
Reading comprehension strategies
Writing skills for different purposes and audiences
Speaking and listening in various contexts
Study skills and learning strategies
In-class support
Individual learning plans ensure all teachers understand each EAL learner’s needs and appropriate support strategies. Our EAL teachers work closely with all subject teachers to monitor EAL learners, ensuring they can fully access the curriculum and gain necessary subject specific support where needed.
In-class support might include
Modified texts or vocabulary lists
Visual aids and concrete resources
Collaborative learning with supportive peers
Additional time for processing and responding
Alternative ways of demonstrating understanding
Examination support
As children progress through Windlesham House, the EAL department can assist with internal and external examinations. We provide examination technique guidance and support applications for access arrangements where appropriate. We also prepare pupils for Cambridge ESOL examinations if families wish to obtain formal English language qualifications.
How does cultural integration support language learning?
Language enrichment activities
To complement traditional learning methods, we organize cultural trips and experiences. This exposure to British life helps children apply language skills and gain deeper cultural understanding of their environment. From visiting museums and nature spots to watching shows and playing sport, children at Windlesham House are introduced to new experiences which enhance their understanding and embed language skills and knowledge.
Peer support and friendships
Immersion in an English-speaking environment provides constant opportunities for language practice. Form groups and boarding houses are deliberately international, creating natural contexts for communication. Pupils develop genuine friendships across cultural and linguistic backgrounds, providing both motivation and opportunity for language development.
Celebrating diversity
We celebrate our international community through assemblies, cultural days and language showcases. Pupils share their home languages and cultures with peers, building mutual respect and understanding. This inclusive approach helps international pupils feel valued for their linguistic and cultural backgrounds while motivating them to develop English proficiency.
What level of English is required for entry?
We welcome pupils at various stages of English language development. For very young pupils (Reception to Year 3), limited English is not a barrier as they learn language naturally through immersion alongside curriculum content.
For older pupils (Years 4 to 8), we typically require at least basic conversational English to ensure pupils can participate in lessons and form friendships quickly. During the admissions process, we assess English level and discuss appropriate support. Our experience shows that motivated pupils make rapid progress with good support structures.
Is there an additional charge for EAL support?
Yes, individual and small group EAL lessons incur an additional charge. The cost depends on the frequency and number of lessons required per week. We discuss EAL needs and associated costs with families before pupils start. In class support and differentiation are included in standard fees.
How long do pupils typically need EAL support?
This varies considerably depending on starting English level, age, first language, and individual aptitude. Younger pupils typically achieve fluency within one to two years. Older pupils might need two to three years to develop academic English proficiency sufficient for independent learning. We review needs regularly and adjust provision accordingly.
Can EAL pupils take entrance examinations for senior schools?
Yes, many of our EAL pupils successfully gain places at competitive senior schools. We prepare them carefully for entrance examinations and work with senior schools to ensure they understand pupils’ language learning journeys. Some senior schools offer modified entrance procedures or additional language support which we help families navigate.
Cambridge ESOL examinations
We can enter pupils for Cambridge English qualifications (PET, FCE, CAE) which provide internationally recognized certification of English language proficiency. These qualifications can be valuable for future education or employment opportunities.
Discussing EAL needs
For conversation about your child’s English language level and appropriate support, please contact our admissions team at whsadmissions@windlesham.com or call +44 (0)1903 874700. We welcome international families and have extensive experience supporting pupils from diverse linguistic backgrounds.

pageCache.pageTitle: Years 7 & 8 diploma programme | Windlesham House School
pageCache.text:
Our distinctive diploma pathways for senior pupils
The Windlesham House Diploma Programme is our distinctive offering for Years 7 & 8, providing breadth and depth beyond the standard curriculum. Pupils explore diverse pathways while preparing excellently for senior school.
What is the Windlesham House Diploma Programme?
The Diploma Programme enhances the core curriculum for our oldest pupils with additional subjects, extended projects and opportunities to develop specialized interests. All Years 7 & 8 pupils participate in the diploma, choosing pathways that align with their strengths and aspirations.
The programme recognizes that pupils in these years are developing more sophisticated interests and preparing for the increased independence of senior school. It provides structure for deeper exploration while developing essential skills for lifelong learning.
What are the diploma components?
English, maths, science and computing pathways
The taught diploma components in English, maths, science and computing will
Provide a strong foundation in all subjects
Be excellent preparation for GCSE
Humanities pathways
Pupils develop specialization in history, geography or religious studies through extended research projects. Recent diploma projects have explored topics ranging from the causes of World War One to sustainable development challenges around the world. Projects develop independent research skills, critical analysis and academic writing.
Languages, Culture, and Linguistics (LCL) diploma
Our innovative LCL diploma takes language learning beyond communication skills to explore linguistics and global culture. Pupils study
This unique approach prepares pupils excellently for modern foreign language studies at senior school while developing analytical and research skills applicable across disciplines.
Performing arts and physical education pathways
Pupils with particular aptitude or interest in art, drama or music can pursue diploma pathways in these subjects. This involves
Extended portfolio or performance work
Study of practitioners, movements and techniques
Critical reflection on creative processes and outcomes
Build confidence and public speaking skills
Scholarship preparations pathways
Lessons for life
Leadership and team spirit
Personal development
Community responsibility
Outdoor education
How does the diploma programme work in practice?
Timetable structure
Diploma sessions are timetabled alongside the core curriculum. Pupils have dedicated diploma time each week where they work on extended projects, attend specialist sessions, or pursue independent research with mentor support.
Choice and flexibility
Pupils choose diploma pathways in consultation with teachers and parents, typically at the start of Year 7. Choices can be adjusted if interests change or new strengths emerge. Most pupils select two to three diploma pathways aligned with their strengths and interests.
Assessment and recognition
Diploma work is assessed through a combination of project work, presentations and examinations. Pupils receive detailed feedback on their progress. Successful completion of diploma pathways is recognized through certificates presented at the end of Year 8. Diploma achievements are reported to senior schools as part of pupil references.
What are the benefits of the diploma programme?
Breadth and depth
Pupils explore subjects beyond standard curriculum requirements while developing deeper understanding in areas of strength and interest.
Senior school preparation
The diploma develops independent learning skills essential for success at senior school and beyond
Personal interests
Pupils have space to pursue genuine interests rather than following a one-size-fits-all programme
Scholarship advantage
Diploma work provides excellent preparation for scholarship examinations and interviews
What recent diploma projects have pupils completed?
Recent diploma projects demonstrate the range and quality of pupil work
Linguistics Investigation of language evolution using computational analysis of historical texts
History Oral history project interviewing local World War Two veterans
Geography Fieldwork study of coastal erosion on the Sussex coast with recommendations for management
Science Design and testing of water filtration systems for developing world contexts
Art Series of paintings exploring identity through portraiture, culminating in gallery exhibition
Music Composition of original pieces for different instrumental combinations with live performances
Is the diploma programme compulsory?
Yes, all Years 7 & 8 pupils participate in the diploma programme. This ensures every pupil benefits from the enhanced curriculum and develops independent learning skills. Pupils choose their specific pathways based on interests and strengths.
How is diploma work different from regular homework?
Diploma projects involve extended investigations over weeks or months rather than short homework tasks. Pupils have greater autonomy in choosing focus areas and research methods. The work is more open-ended, requiring creativity and independent decision-making alongside academic skills.
Do senior schools recognize diploma qualifications?
While the diploma is a Windlesham House qualification rather than an externally examined award, senior schools value the skills and experiences it represents. We include diploma achievements in pupil references and often discuss diploma work during senior school interviews. The programme provides excellent material for scholarship portfolios and interview discussions.
Diploma information
For more detailed information about diploma pathways and recent pupil projects, please contact the diploma coordinator via whsoffice@windlesham.com.

pageCache.pageTitle: Performing arts | Independent School | Windlesham House School
pageCache.text:
Music, drama, and creative expression for all
The performing arts are central to life at Windlesham House, providing opportunities for creative expression, confidence building, and pure joy. Whether performing in our 250-seat theatre, singing in choirs, or learning musical instruments, pupils discover their creative potential and develop skills that last a lifetime.
What music opportunities are available?
Classroom music
All pupils receive curriculum music lessons taught by specialist teachers. These lessons cover:
Singing and vocal technique
Rhythm and percussion
Listening and appreciation
Music theory and notation
Composition and creativity
World music and different genres
Musical instruments and orchestral families
Individual instrumental lessons
We offer individual or small-group lessons in a wide range of instruments including:
Lessons are taught by experienced peripatetic teachers, many of whom are professional musicians. Pupils can start learning instruments from as young as Reception, with guidance provided on the best instruments for different ages.
We have an impressive statistic: over 100 pupils learn musical instruments at any given time, reflecting how many families in our community play instruments. This creates a wonderfully musical atmosphere at Windlesham House.
Woodwind Flute, clarinet, oboe, bassoon, saxophone, recorder
Brass Trumpet, cornet, horn, trombone, tuba, euphonium
Keyboard Piano, keyboard, organ
Percussion Drums, orchestral percussion, marimba
Voice Singing lessons
Choirs and ensembles
Pupils can join various musical groups:
These groups rehearse regularly and perform at school concerts, providing valuable ensemble experience and the thrill of making music together.
Orchestra Full orchestra for instrumental players
String ensemble For string players
Wind band Woodwind and brass players
Rock band Contemporary music group
Concerts and performances
Throughout the year, we hold numerous concerts and musical showcases:
These performances build confidence, stage presence, and resilience. Overcoming performance nerves and sharing music with audiences are valuable life skills.
Informal performances Lunchtime concerts, assemblies, special occasions
What drama opportunities exist?
Curriculum drama
Drama is part of the curriculum for all pupils, teaching:
Drama lessons use games, exercises, and scripted work to develop skills progressively from Reception through Year 8.
Voice projection and articulation
Movement and physicality
Character development
Improvisation and creativity
Script work and text analysis
Stagecraft and technical theatre
Confidence and public speaking
School productions
Major school productions each year provide opportunities for pupils to perform in our professional 250-seat Malden Family Theatre. Recent productions have included:
Productions involve not just actors but also:
This inclusive approach means many pupils can be involved even if they do not wish to act. The collaborative nature of theatre teaches teamwork, responsibility, and commitment.
Around the World in 80 Days
Macbeth in the Woods (outdoor production)
West End showcases
Musical theatre productions
Stage crew and technicians (lighting, sound)
Costume and makeup teams
Set designers and painters
Programme creators
Front of house teams
Drama clubs and activities
Beyond curriculum drama and productions, pupils can participate in:
Drama club (after school)
Public speaking competitions
Improvisation workshops
Theatre trips to professional productions
LAMDA examinations
We offer LAMDA lessons where pupils work towards graded examinations in:
LAMDA qualifications are recognized by UCAS and develop skills in communication, confidence, and performance that benefit pupils in all areas of life.
Reading for performance
Speaking in public
Musical theatre
What facilities support performing arts?
Malden Family Theatre
Our magnificent 250-seat theatre features:
This professional venue allows pupils to experience real theatre craft and perform to high standards.
Professional lighting rig
Sound system and mixing desk
Large stage with backstage areas
Orchestra pit
Dressing rooms
Lighting and sound technician (available on request)
Drama studio
A dedicated drama studio with tiered seating and AV equipment provides space for lessons, rehearsals, and smaller performances.
Music rooms
Multiple music practice rooms and teaching spaces ensure individual lessons and group rehearsals can happen simultaneously. Soundproofing means pupils can practice without disturbing classes.
We have a piano in our historic Chapel and organ, providing beautiful settings for musical performances during services and concerts.
How do performing arts benefit pupils?
Confidence and communication
Performing in front of audiences builds self-assurance and presentation skills valuable in all future contexts from job interviews to leading teams.
Creativity and expression
The arts provide outlets for emotions, ideas, and imagination. Many pupils who struggle academically shine in performing arts, discovering talents they did not know they had.
Discipline and perseverance
Learning instruments or preparing for productions requires practice, patience, and commitment. These experiences teach that mastery comes through effort, building work ethic and resilience.
Collaboration and empathy
Ensemble music-making and theatre productions require working with others towards common goals. Pupils learn to listen, compromise, support castmates, and understand different perspectives.
Cultural appreciation
Exposure to music and drama from different cultures, periods, and styles broadens horizons and develops cultural literacy.
Joy and wellbeing
Perhaps most importantly, performing arts bring joy. The excitement of performances, the satisfaction of learning a new piece, and the fun of creating with friends contribute enormously to pupil wellbeing and happy school memories.
Does my child need to audition for productions?
Major speaking and singing roles may require auditions, but we always find ways for all interested pupils to be involved whether through acting, chorus, technical crew, or other roles. We believe theatre is for everyone and structure productions to maximize participation.
How much does music tuition cost?
Individual instrumental lessons are charged per lesson as extras to school fees. Pricing varies depending on lesson length and whether individual or shared lessons. Group activities like choirs and ensembles are included in school fees. Details of music tuition costs are available from the school office.
Can pupils hire instruments?
Yes, the school can arrange instrument hire for most instruments, particularly larger or more expensive instruments like cellos, bassoons, and tubas. This allows pupils to try instruments before committing to purchase. Piano and keyboards are available at school for practice.
What if my child is shy about performing?
We never force pupils to perform but gently encourage and build confidence gradually. Many initially shy pupils surprise themselves by discovering they enjoy performing once they try. Drama lessons include confidence-building exercises in safe, supportive environments. Some pupils prefer technical roles or audience participation rather than starring roles, and that is absolutely fine.
Recent performances
Our summer musical showcase and productions like Macbeth in the Woods have showcased the incredible talent of our pupils. Little musicians in pre-prep also shine in regular performances. Check our website news section for videos and photos of recent performances.
Alumni success
Many Windlesham House alumni have pursued performing arts careers or maintained music and drama as important parts of their lives. The foundation built here serves pupils whether they become professional performers or simply appreciate the arts as adults.
At Windlesham House, we don’t simply prepare children for the future, we give them a childhood worth remembering. Discover a school where curiosity is nurtured, every child is genuinely known and childhood is celebrated every day.

pageCache.pageTitle: Charterhouse family of schools | Windlesham House School
pageCache.text:
What is the Charterhouse family of schools?
Windlesham House is part of the Charterhouse family of schools (registered charity 312054). The governing body of Charterhouse has responsibility for all schools, but each school is run independently, retaining their own identity, name and ethos, as well as their day-to-day operational autonomy.
The Charterhouse family of schools brings together several prep and pre-prep schools with the senior school at its heart. This relationship allows us to share best practices, resources and expertise while maintaining our unique identity and character as the oldest prep school in the country.
What benefits does this partnership bring?
Educational excellence
Being part of the Charterhouse family allows us to collaborate on curriculum development, teaching approaches and educational innovation. We share ideas with other schools in the family, attend joint training sessions and benefit from the expertise of a wider educational community.
Smooth transition
For families considering Charterhouse as a senior school option, our affiliation provides reassurance and continuity. While Windlesham House pupils go on to a wide range of senior schools, those choosing Charterhouse benefit from our close relationship and understanding of their expectations.
Shared values
The Charterhouse family of schools shares common values around academic excellence, outstanding pastoral care and developing well-rounded individuals. This alignment strengthens our approach and connects our community to a wider educational vision.
Staff development and resources
Our staff benefit from professional development opportunities within the Charterhouse family, including joint training days, subject-specific networks and leadership development programmes. This ensures our teaching remains at the forefront of educational practice.
Inter-school activities
Pupils across the Charterhouse family participate in joint events, competitions and activities. These opportunities include sports fixtures, music concerts, academic challenges and social events, enriching the school experience.
How does Windlesham House maintain its independence?
The Charterhouse family of schools partnership enhances our offering while we maintain our unique identity as the oldest prep school in the UK with our own rich heritage and distinctive approach to education.
While we value our Charterhouse affiliation, Windlesham House School remains proudly independent with our own distinct character, traditions and approach. Being part of the Charterhouse family of schools enhances rather than defines who we are.
We continue to prepare pupils for the full range of senior schools, not just Charterhouse. Our focus remains on finding the right school for each individual child, whether that is Charterhouse or one of the many other excellent schools our pupils attend.
At Windlesham House, we don’t simply prepare children for the future, we give them a childhood worth remembering. Discover a school where curiosity is nurtured, every child is genuinely known and childhood is celebrated every day.

pageCache.pageTitle: Our history | Prep School Pulborough | Windlesham House School
pageCache.text:
Where is Windlesham House School located?
Windlesham House School is nestled in the heart of the South Downs National Park in West Sussex, just over an hour from London. Our magnificent seventy-acre estate sits on the site of the historic Windlesham House, surrounded by rolling countryside, ancient woodland and stunning natural beauty.
The school is easily accessible from Brighton, Worthing, Chichester and London, making it an ideal choice for both day pupils and boarders. Our private estate setting provides a safe, inspiring environment where children can learn, play and grow surrounded by nature.
A unique South Downs setting
Our location within the South Downs National Park gives pupils daily access to one of England’s most beautiful landscapes. The rolling hills, woodland and open spaces become an extension of our classroom, supporting outdoor learning, forest school activities and a genuine connection with nature.
The peaceful countryside setting provides the perfect balance – close enough to major cities for convenience, yet far enough away to offer children the freedom, space and fresh air that is increasingly rare in today’s busy world.
How has Windlesham House evolved since 1837?
Windlesham House School was established in 1837, making us one of the oldest preps school in the country. For nearly two centuries, we have been at the forefront of preparatory education, constantly evolving to meet the needs of each new generation while maintaining our commitment to academic excellence and pastoral care.
Pioneering spirit
Throughout our history, Windlesham House has been a pioneer in independent education. We were among the first prep schools to embrace co-education, welcoming girls in 1967. This forward-thinking approach has always been part of our character, honouring tradition while having the courage to innovate.
Our decision not to have a school uniform, introduced to help boarding pupils feel more at home, reflects our understanding that children thrive when they feel comfortable and can express their individuality. This distinctive choice has become one of our defining features.
Continuous development
Over the decades, we have invested continuously in our facilities and teaching approaches. From our state-of-the-art science laboratories and sports centre to our beautiful chapel and performing arts spaces, we have created an environment that supports twenty-first-century learning while preserving the best of our heritage.
Who leads the school and what is their vision?
Windlesham House School is led by Sophie Baber, our Head, who has joined the school with a clear vision for combining academic excellence with outstanding pastoral care and a rich co-curricular programme.
Under Sophie’s leadership, the school continues to build on its distinguished heritage while embracing innovation in teaching and learning. Her vision centres on developing confident, independent young people who are prepared not just for their next school but for life in an ever-changing world.
Leadership team
Supporting the Head is an experienced senior leadership team, including the senior deputy head, deputy head (academic), interim head of pre-prep, business manager and bursar. Together, they ensure that every aspect of school life reflects our values and maintains the highest standards.
What role does the chapel play in school life?
The Windlesham House chapel is at the heart of our school community. While we welcome families of all faiths and none, the chapel provides a beautiful, peaceful space for reflection, celebration and coming together as a community.
Community gatherings
We hold regular assemblies in the chapel where we celebrate achievements, share stories and reinforce our school values. These gatherings help create a strong sense of community and belonging, allowing children to reflect on their experiences and learn from one another.
Special occasions
Throughout the year, the chapel hosts special services and concerts, from our Christmas carol service to end-of-term celebrations. These occasions bring together pupils, staff and families in a space that has witnessed generations of Windlesham House children growing and flourishing.
What makes Windlesham House’s heritage special?
As the oldest prep school in the UK, Windlesham House has nearly two hundred years of experience in preparing children for success, combining time-honoured traditions with modern innovation.
Established excellence
Since 1837, we have built a reputation for outstanding education and exceptional pastoral care that families trust.
Pioneering spirit
We were the first prep school to become co-educational and continue to lead in educational innovation.
Strong foundation
Our long history provides stability and wisdom, ensuring tried-and-tested approaches alongside modern methods.
Alumni success
Generations of Windlesham House pupils have gone on to excel at top senior schools and in their chosen careers.
Continuous evolution
We have grown and adapted over nearly two centuries while staying true to our core commitment to each child’s development.
At Windlesham House, we don’t simply prepare children for the future, we give them a childhood worth remembering. Discover a school where curiosity is nurtured, every child is genuinely known and childhood is celebrated every day.

Windlesham House offers EAL immersive short stay programmes that allow pupils to experience authentic British prep school life. These programmes provide a wonderful opportunity for children to improve their English, make international friends, and sample the benefits of boarding education.
Short stay pupils are fully integrated into school life, attending lessons, participating in activities and living alongside our full-time pupils. This immersive approach ensures they gain genuine insight into what makes Windlesham House special.
These courses provide a greater prep boarding experience and all our pupils thrive from the diversity shared in the classroom and boarding houses. Term-time immersion courses typically last from two weeks to one full term, depending on family requirements.
